Strictly additive: new `Peripheral` / `ProtocolProject` dataclasses, new `build_protocol_schematic()`, new symbol pin tables, `PROTOCOL_PROJECTS`, `ALL_PROJECTS`. The existing `Project` / `build_schematic` / `build_board` path and every existing symbol table are untouched — `write_project` dispatches on `isinstance(project, ProtocolProject)`, and `main()` now iterates `ALL_PROJECTS` so `--project` accepts the new names.

### Symbol 1 — `MCU:ESP32-DEVKITC-32` (value `ESP32-DEVKITC-32`, ref `U1`)

`lib_id` contains "esp32" so `_is_controller` fires on the lib hint, not just the pin heuristic.

| # | name | etype | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3V3 | power_in | listed first so `_supply_net` returns the +3V3 rail, not GND |
| 2 | GND | power_in | |
| 5 | GPIO5 | bidirectional | classic ESP32 VSPI CS |
| 18 | GPIO18 | bidirectional | VSPI SCK |
| 19 | GPIO19 | bidirectional | VSPI MISO |
| 21 | GPIO21 | bidirectional | I2C SDA default |
| 22 | GPIO22 | bidirectional | I2C SCL default |
| 23 | GPIO23 | bidirectional | VSPI MOSI |
| 25 | GPIO25 | bidirectional | spare GPIO |
| 30 | SCK | output | controller drives clock |
| 31 | MOSI | output | controller drives data out |
| 32 | MISO | input | controller listens |
| 33 | CS | output | controller drives select |
| 34 | TX | output | |
| 35 | RX | input | |
| 36 | EN | input | tied to +3V3, mirrors the existing fixture idiom |

Two deliberate choices:
- **Pin numbers mirror the GPIO number** (`GPIO18` is pin `"18"`). `Component.pin()` matches name *or* number, so with 1..16 numbering `pin("5")` would have returned `GPIO19`. Alias pins sit on 30–36, outside `{5,18,19,21,22,23,25}`, so name- and number-resolution can never disagree.
- **Both matching paths coexist on the same symbol**: alias-matching finds literal `SCK`/`MOSI`/`MISO`/`CS`/`TX`/`RX`, and the explicit-answer path (or a `default_controller_pin="GPIO18"`) finds the plain GPIOs. Verified: `_answered_pin(u1,"GPIO25")`, `("25")`, `("18:GPIO18")` all resolve; the clarification option list `[p.name for p in pins if CONTROLLER_PIN_HINT.match(p.name)]` yields exactly the 7 GPIOs.

### Symbol 2 — `Display:ILI9341` (value `ILI9341`, SPI peripheral)
`1 VCC power_in`, `2 GND power_in`, `3 SCK input`, `4 MOSI input`, `5 MISO output`, `6 CS input`. MISO is a real `output`, which is the whole point: it makes "reject only when BOTH endpoints are outputs" distinguishable from the I2C "reject any output" rule.

### Symbol 3 — `RF:HC-05` (value `HC-05`, UART peripheral)
`1 VCC power_in`, `2 GND power_in`, `3 TX output`, `4 RX input`. The crossover `U1.TX(output) -> U2.RX(input)` and `U1.RX(input) -> U2.TX(output)` are both electrically valid; `TX->TX` would be two outputs.

### Symbol 4 — `Relay:RELAY_2CH` (value `RELAY-2CH`, GPIO peripheral)
`1 VCC power_in`, `2 GND power_in`, `3 IN1 input`, `4 IN2 input`, `5 FAULT output`. No aliasable signal names at all, so GPIO must ask for both pins. `IN1`/`IN2` do not match `^(GPIO|IO|P[A-D])\d+$`, so it stays a peripheral. Answer forms `"3:IN1"`, `"IN1"`, `"3"` all resolve to `IN1`.

### Symbol 5 — `Device:Fan` (value `FAN_5015`, power-only)
`1 VCC power_in`, `2 GND power_in`. Nothing else.

**Both-outputs rejection pair the next agent needs:** `U1.TX` (output) ↔ `U2.FAULT` (output) in `esp32_gpio_peripheral`, or `U1.TX` ↔ `U2.MISO` (output) in `esp32_spi_display`. Valid-direction pairs: `U1.SCK/MOSI/CS (output) -> U2.SCK/MOSI/CS (input)`, `U2.MISO (output) -> U1.MISO (input)`.

## New projects (all `U1` = MCU, `U2` = peripheral, `.kicad_sch` + `.kicad_pro`, no `.kicad_pcb`)

| project | components | nets |
|---|---|---|
| `esp32_spi_display` | U1, U2 (ILI9341), #PWR01/02, #FLG01/02 | `+3V3`, `GND` |
| `esp32_uart_module` | U1, U2 (HC-05), + power | `+3V3`, `GND` |
| `esp32_gpio_peripheral` | U1, U2 (RELAY-2CH), + power | `+3V3`, `GND` |
| `esp32_power_only` | U1, U2 (FAN_5015), + power | `+3V3`, `GND` |

The peripheral is entirely unwired in all four — that is the planner's work. **The MCU must stay in `esp32_power_only`:** the reader skips power-symbol pins when building `nets`, so `+3V3`/`GND` only become resolvable by `_resolve_rail` because the MCU's `3V3`/`GND` pin labels put them there. Trim U1 and every POWER plan fails with `incompatible_voltage`. Confirmed for all four: `_is_controller(U1)=True`, `_is_controller(U2)=False`, `_supply_net(U1)="+3V3"` (== rail, so no `incompatible_logic_voltage`), `VCC`/`GND` resolve on every peripheral.

**No `.kicad_pcb` on the new projects** — one dedicated board fixture (`esp32_i2c_board`) is the pattern, and `build_board` is hardcoded to the ESP32/TMP102/USB footprints.

## ⚠️ Collision the next agent must know about

`SCL_NAMES = ("SCL","SCK","I2C_SCL","CLK")` in `generator.py`, and resolution order puts `_pin_by_names` **before** the `GPIO22` default. Verified: on the new MCU, `_pin_by_names(u1, SCL_NAMES) -> "SCK"` (pin 30, an `output`). So an **I2C** plan against any of the four new fixtures resolves SCL to an output pin and gets rejected by the I2C `shared_outputs_forbidden` rule, never reaching the GPIO22 default. Do not run I2C against the new fixtures. I kept the name `SCK` because the task requires the alias path to be testable; renaming to `SCLK` would break it. The five I2C fixtures use the old `MCU:ESP32-WROOM-32` symbol and are completely unaffected.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("app/kicad/erc.py")
t = p.read_text()

anchor = '''    def _run_check(self, subcommand: list[str], target: Path, extra: list[str] | None = None) -> ErcReport:'''
new = '''    def run_drc_baseline(self, board: Path, passes: int = 2) -> ErcReport:
        """A DRC baseline that is a conservative superset of any single run.

        KiCAD's DRC is not fully deterministic. On a byte-identical board it
        intermittently reports one or two fewer violations - measured here as 20
        violations on 38 of 40 runs, 19 once and 18 once, with kicad-cli's own
        output saying "Found 8 violations" one run and "Found 7" the next. The
        ones that come and go are clearance violations, which `_awaiting_routing`
        does not exempt.

        That matters because whichever run happens to become the baseline decides
        whether a later, normal run looks like it introduced new errors. A
        single-run baseline therefore makes the DRC gate reject valid work at
        random, roughly one time in twenty. Unioning a couple of passes fixes the
        dangerous direction: a violation KiCAD reported on the original board is
        pre-existing no matter which pass found it, so it can never be counted as
        new later. It cannot hide a real regression either - a violation the
        original board does not have cannot appear in any pass over it.
        """
        report = self.run_drc(board)
        if not report.ran or passes < 2:
            return report
        seen = {v.signature() for v in report.violations}
        merged = list(report.violations)
        for _ in range(passes - 1):
            extra_pass = self.run_drc(board)
            if not extra_pass.ran:
                continue
            for violation in extra_pass.violations:
                if violation.signature() not in seen:
                    seen.add(violation.signature())
                    merged.append(violation)
        return report.model_copy(
            update={
                "violations": merged,
                "errors": sum(1 for v in merged if v.severity == "error"),
                "warnings": sum(1 for v in merged if v.severity == "warning"),
            }
        )

    def _run_check(self, subcommand: list[str], target: Path, extra: list[str] | None = None) -> ErcReport:'''
assert anchor in t
p.write_text(t.replace(anchor, new, 1))
print("erc.py patched")

content.text:
Every number in your runbook still holds exactly — baseline ERC 10 err · 8 warn, baseline DRC 5 err · 13 warn, accepted, 9/9 checks, 6/6 connections, ERC 10 → 1. No runbook edits needed.

**Wave 1 done, wave 2 running.** The fixtures agent delivered and flagged two hazards rather than hiding them — that report was genuinely good. Committed: a richer MCU (GPIO5/18/19/21/22/23/25 plus SCK/MOSI/MISO/CS/TX/RX aliases) and four peripherals — SPI display, UART module, a relay with deliberately no aliasable pin names, and a two-pin fan. Electrical types are realistic on purpose: the display's MISO is a real output, which is what makes "reject only when *both* endpoints are outputs" testable versus the I2C rule that rejects any output on the bus. The protocol-engine agent is now building against them.

**I found and fixed two real bugs while waiting, and one of them would have bitten you on stage.**

The important one: `test_drc_diffing_is_deterministic` was failing about one full-suite run in three. It wasn't a flaky test — it asserted something false. On a byte-identical board, `kicad-cli` reports 20 violations on 38 of 40 runs, 19 once, 18 once; its own output says "Found 8 violations" one run and "Found 7" the next. `ran` is `True` every time, so nothing downstream could tell. The ones that come and go are *clearance* violations, which the unrouted-board exemption doesn't cover.

Why that's a safety bug, not a curiosity: whichever run becomes the baseline decides whether a later normal run looks like it introduced errors. Your demo plan syncs the board, which makes DRC a real gate — so **a valid change was getting rejected at random, roughly one time in twenty, on the demo project.** `run_drc_baseline` now unions a couple of passes at both baseline sites, so a violation KiCad reported on the original board is pre-existing whichever pass found it. It can't hide a real regression either: a violation the original board doesn't have can't appear in a pass over it. That pair of test files failed ~1 in 5 before; it's now 6/6 clean.

The second: a bare `python3 scripts/make_fixtures.py` **deleted four committed `.kicad_pcb` files** — `rmtree` wiped the directory but only `board=True` projects get a board rebuilt, and those four came from the board-sync work. Anyone regenerating fixtures before the demo would have silently broken the board sync and the board-sync tests. Now it overwrites only what it generates: 5 boards before, 5 after, zero deletions.

Also committed earlier: 8 tests for the LLM path, which had never executed.

I replaced that false determinism test rather than deleting it, and I want to be explicit since it's the one place I changed an existing test's meaning: the replacement asserts what actually has to hold — nothing a single pass may look new against the baseline — plus union semantics and the not-ran case, and net-keyed unconnected signatures keep their own separate test.

I'll report when the protocol engine lands, with the acceptance gates run.

The planner is one algorithm; a protocol is data. Each :class:`SignalSpec` says
what a signal is called on the *controller* and on the *peripheral* separately.
That per-side split is what expresses UART's TX/RX crossover without any special
case, and it is what stops an I2C ``SCL`` request from resolving to an MCU's
``SCK`` output (which is SPI's clock, not I2C's).

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)

    peripheral_names: tuple[str, ...]

    default_controller_pin: str | None = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProtocolSpec:
    protocol: Protocol
    net_prefix: str
    signals: tuple[SignalSpec, ...]
    pullup_signals: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    shared_outputs_forbidden: bool = True

    def signal(self, name: str) -> SignalSpec | None:
        for signal in self.signals:
            if signal.name == name:
                return signal
        return None

            peripheral_names=("SDA", "SDIO", "I2C_SDA", "DATA"),
            purpose="I2C data",
            default_controller_pin="GPIO21",
        ),
        # `SCK` is deliberately absent from the controller aliases: on an MCU
        # symbol that pin is the SPI clock and an output. Peripherals that really
        # do label their I2C clock SCK are still matched, last.
        SignalSpec(
            name="SCL",
            controller_names=("SCL", "I2C_SCL"),
            peripheral_names=("SCL", "I2C_SCL", "CLK", "SCK"),

UART_SPEC = ProtocolSpec(

    net_prefix="UART",
    signals=(
        SignalSpec(
            name="TX",
            controller_names=("TX", "TXD", "UART_TX", "TXO"),
            peripheral_names=("RX", "RXD", "UART_RX", "RXI"),

)

# No aliases and no default: both ends of a GPIO connection must be answered.
GPIO_SPEC = ProtocolSpec(
    protocol=Protocol.GPIO,
    net_prefix="NET",
    signals=(
        SignalSpec(

            controller_names=(),

Implement §7: SPI, UART, GPIO and simple power connections

The planner is now one algorithm and a protocol is data. `protocols.py`
holds a SignalSpec per signal naming it separately on the controller and on
the peripheral, which is what expresses UART's TX/RX crossover with no
special case at all — the controller's TX is wired to whatever the
peripheral calls RX. No new action types were needed: SPI, UART, GPIO and
power all decompose into the existing connect_pins / connect_pin_to_net /
ensure_pullup, so §12's fixed schema and the four Mitos tools still cover
execution.

The per-side split also fixes a real collision. `SCL_NAMES` contained
"SCK" and was used for both ends, so an I2C request against an MCU that
also has SPI resolved SCL to the SCK pin — an output. I2C's controller
aliases no longer include SCK; peripherals that genuinely label their I2C
clock SCK still match, last.

The validator's output rule is now protocol-aware, which is the subtle
part: I2C is open-drain so any output on the bus is a fault, while on
SPI/UART a controller output driving a peripheral input is the normal case
and only output-against-output is a conflict. Verified both directions.

Also §13's missing half: an existing pull-up is now checked for an
acceptable value (1k-10k) rather than accepted merely for bridging net to
rail, and an out-of-range one is warned about and supplemented rather than
silently trusted or deleted.

PlanAnswers gains controller_pins/peripheral_pins dicts and folds the four
legacy I2C scalars into them, so existing clients and the current frontend
keep working untouched. That change also required llm.py to switch to
exclude_defaults: the new dicts default to {}, which is not None, so
exclude_none would have made every request look answered and quietly
stopped the LLM ever being called.

One existing test was replaced rather than fixed: it asserted SPI is
refused as an unsupported protocol, which §7 makes false. It now asserts
the behaviour that matters — SPI against a part with no SPI pins asks which
pin carries the signal instead of pressing SDA into service as MOSI — and a
new test keeps the unsupported-protocol guard covered through an answer the
parser cannot produce.

Let the UI answer the per-signal clarifications §7 introduced

Clarifications for protocols beyond I2C name their signal in the key —
"peripheral_pin:GPIO", "controller_pin:SCK" — but page.tsx wrote every
answer flat as `answers[answer_key]`, and PlanAnswers ignores unknown
fields. So the answer was silently dropped and the same question came back
forever: SPI, UART and GPIO were unusable through the browser even though
the planner handled them correctly.

A namespaced key now routes into controller_pins/peripheral_pins. I2C's
four legacy scalar keys are untouched.

Verified in a real browser against fresh code: esp32_gpio_peripheral asks
which peripheral pin carries the signal, then which controller pin, then
renders a 3-action plan (U2.IN1 <-> U1.GPIO5 as NET_GPIO5, power, ground).
Two distinct questions, two answers, plan reached — no repeat. No layout
change was needed; the plan preview renders a new protocol as-is.
